Field surveys of Common silver-biddy (Gerres subfasciatus) in the coastal waters of eastern Australia have provided detailed morphometric data for this abundant gerreid species. Examination of a large sample of adults revealed that the ultimate standard length reaches approximately 20 centimeters [Li = approximately 20 centimeters], representing the maximum size attained by individuals in this population. The relationship between length and body mass was derived from a comprehensive collection of specimens, allowing estimation of the ultimate wet weight at about 137.4 grams [Wwi = about 137.4 grams] for a fish of maximal length. This asymptotic body mass is consistent with values reported for other gerreids of comparable body shape. Juvenile individuals were also measured extensively, and the standard length at puberty was determined to be 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters], marking the size at which gonadal development begins. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from the length-mass allometry, is 12 grams [Wwp = 12 grams], a modest body size that reflects the relatively early reproductive investment observed in this species compared to some larger-bodied congeners.

The early life stages of Gerres subfasciatus are characterized by a remarkably small initial size at birth. Based on the typical egg diameter of 0.5 millimeters for this species, the wet weight at birth is estimated to be 0.0000654 grams [Wwb = 0.0000654 grams], a value that reflects the minute, yolk-laden pelagic eggs produced during spawning events. This extremely low neonatal mass is typical of marine teleosts that release large numbers of small, transparent eggs into the plankton. The larval eclosion occurs after a brief incubation period, and the newly emerged yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous nutrients during the lecithotrophic phase. The transition to exogenous feeding marks a critical bottleneck in survival, as first-feeding larvae must encounter suitable prey items within the planktonic environment to avoid starvation. The diminutive size of the hatchling, at just over sixty micrograms, imposes tight constraints on the types of zooplankton that can be successfully captured by the mouth-gape-limited larva.

Reproductive output in Common silver-biddy has been investigated through field collections of gravid females combined with laboratory observations of spawning behavior. Females produce approximately 367200 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 367200 eggs per year] at a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], a high fecundity that reflects a spawning strategy in which multiple batches of pelagic eggs are released over an extended breeding season. The spawning adult is iteroparous, with individuals reproducing repeatedly across successive years. The high annual egg production is among the highest recorded for gerreids of similar body size, underscoring the species capacity for rapid population turnover in response to favorable environmental conditions.

Longevity estimates for Gerres subfasciatus have been derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination conducted in subtropical estuaries. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species is approximately 8.5 years [am = approximately 8.5 years] at a mean annual water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], a duration that is typical for small to medium-sized gerreids inhabiting warm temperate waters. This longevity encompasses a reproductive window of several years, during which individuals can contribute multiple spawning seasons to the population. Age-specific mortality appears to increase markedly after the sixth year, with very few individuals exceeding the eighth year. The relatively moderate lifespan likely reflects a life history strategy that balances early maturation and high fecundity against the energetic costs of sustained reproductive effort in a seasonally variable environment, a pattern consistent with the risk-spawning hypothesis proposed for tropical gerreids.

The life history of Gerres subfasciatus is further shaped by the interplay between its moderate body size and its precise thermal requirements for successful reproduction. The maximum lifespan of 8.5 years [am = 8.5 years] at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C] is closely tied to the species' reliance on warm, productive estuarine habitats, where the extended spawning season allows the annual production of approximately 367200 eggs [Ri = annual production of approximately 367200 eggs] to be sustained. Puberty at a standard length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters] represents an early commitment to reproduction relative to the ultimate length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], a strategy that enhances lifetime fecundity in environments where adult mortality is high. This combination of early maturity, sustained high fecundity, and a moderate lifespan positions Gerres subfasciatus as a classic intermediate strategist within the gerreid clade, well-adapted to the variable conditions of shallow coastal and estuarine environments where it is most abundant.
